tour.title: Three Weeks In: When Grief Takes Your Prayers
tour.intro: You asked to hear people talk honestly about grief and where God is in it — no tidy answers. This tour starts with a father telling the exact moment his son died, then walks through what the Bible's own grieving people did when they had no words: Job cursed the day he was born, the psalmists accused God, and the Spirit, Paul says, groans when we cannot. The voices here don't explain your mother's death away. They hand you back your own honest voice, and then something to do with it. About twenty minutes total; you can stop anywhere.

steps.why: Start with someone who has been where you are. Youth minister Cameron Cole tells the morning his three-year-old son Cameron died — the missed calls, his wife's voice saying 'Cameron is dead' — and what came out of his mouth first: 'Jesus rose from the dead... that means that God's good and this doesn't change that fact.' He is not preaching at you; he is recounting the doctrines that 'felt like they were essential to holding me together' in the first unbearable year, and ending on the raw question 'why is God preserving me?' This is the honest, non-tidy company you asked for.

Now the Bible's own grief. Teaching Job 3 — where Job wishes he had never been born — the hosts point out that Jeremiah curses 'the day when my mother bore me,' that the Bible 'does not read like an instruction book' for grief but shows you 'here's how this sounds when someone is in this situation.' The line to hold onto: 'lament rather than being a signal of the absence of faith is actually a sign that faith is very much present' — 'you don't lament to a God that you think is not there.' If you feel guilty for your worst thoughts, this clip says your crying out is itself faith.

A direct answer to the exact person you are. A listener named Joanna writes that three years after losing her father, she cannot pray: doubt makes prayer feel 'like a silly exercise in talking to myself,' and her grief feels 'selfish and unimportant.' Tom Wright tells her plainly, 'this is not selfish and it is not unimportant. God loves your broken heart as much as he loved your unbroken heart before... God specializes in broken hearts, God's own heart was broken on the cross.' Then he gives her a way in: read the Bethany story slowly, don't hurry to the raising of Lazarus, and let the Psalms be your prayer book — 'Psalm 88, which leaves you in the dark, but with the knowledge that somehow it's God's darkness.'

The theology under the last clip, in a calmer teaching voice: Romans 8, where Paul says plainly 'we don't know how to pray as we should.' The teacher walks the phrase 'the Spirit Himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words' — in Greek, literally 'wordless groanings' — and names your exact state: 'the weight of difficulty, hardship has washed over us so deeply, and we've got nothing left.' His point: at that moment the Spirit takes what you cannot say and 'translates those groanings according to the will of God.' Not being able to pray is not a failure; it is the situation the text was written for.

The closest thing in this tour to an answer to 'where is God in it.' Teaching Isaiah 53 — 'he has borne our griefs and he's carried our sorrows' — the teacher says your feeling that you are 'burying your own griefs and your own sorrows' is real, but 'somebody has carried not just something similar, but that exact thing... your grief and your sorrow is born by Christ.' And the sentence to sit with: 'any idea that you're experiencing these things alone, that nobody else knows about this, is a lie.' No explanation of why she died — just a claim about who is carrying it.

End with a gift you can use tonight. Closing their series on Lamentations, these hosts admit what church often taught them: 'I don't think I've been given permission to complain, yeah, protest, beg, tell God to look and see.' Then they give it back: 'Give yourself permission to lament... find a lament psalm. Go to Psalm 88, go to a part of the book of Lamentations and just pray God's own words back to him. You're in safe ground to do that.' They show how — 'God, I weep bitterly every night, tears are on my cheeks' — and promise 'you can just be yourself with God.' If you cannot find your own words, borrow theirs; the book is full of people who already said it.

tour.closing: Three weeks in, you don't need a conclusion — you need company, and you need to know your silence is not a failure. These voices say it from different rooms: your grief is not too small for God, your not-praying is where the Spirit prays, your worst cries are scripture-shaped faith, and the grief itself has been carried. When you're ready, the last clip leaves you with actual words to try — Psalm 88 or Lamentations, prayed in the first person, spoken to a God who can take it. Your mother is not a problem to be solved. You are just a grieving child, and that is a place God is already in.

caveats: Clips on ad-inserted hosts (Megaphone: ask-nt-wright, spoken-gospel) can land up to ~2 minutes off against today’s stream. This is a known corpus-wide drift, not a bug in this tour.
A tour is model output over machine transcripts. The "why" text should report what a transcript says; it is not a claim that the speaker is right.

The player streams each episode straight from its publisher. A few hosts (Substack’s CDN, for one) refuse hotlinked requests and the step will say so and offer the URL instead — the clip boundaries are still good, the playback path is not.
